Epitaph for Dharma Master Shenwu of Nanying Mountain, Hangzhou The teachings of Tiantai first flourished during the Chen and Sui dynasties.
After the death of the Patriarch, during the Tang dynasty, the schools of *xìng* (nature) and *xiàng* (phenomena) spread widely throughout the north and south;
heterodox views arose and the subtle words [of the Buddha] were nearly extinguished. It was the Chan Master Jingxi who declined these errors and cleared away the obstructions.
Consequently, the [teachings] were revived and flourished in Jingxi after having been extinguished;

yet by the time of our Song dynasty, several hundred years had passed, and scholars rarely grasped the essential points, with disputes over right and wrong leading to increasingly severe errors and contradictions. There appeared a great teacher known as Shenwu (Divine Awakening);
his secular name was Changjing, his courtesy name Zhongqian, and he was a native of Yongjia. From his youth, he grew weary of worldly rituals and resided at Shangneng Temple.

His teacher was the thirteenth patriarch of the Tiantai school, who himself had shaved his head, received the precepts, and traveled abroad to study before finally setting foot at the gate of Ciyun at Tiantong Temple in Qiantang.

[The master] was exceptionally sharp and transcended his peers; his excellent reputation overflowed beyond his immediate circle, such that both senior and junior practitioners were struck with awe and submitted in respectful admiration.
Subsequently, he traveled to various regions to seek instruction, yet finding that the Way did not accord with them, he finally arrived at...
At Tiantai Daye Mountain, he encountered Dharma Master Shenzhao; serving him with devotion at his feet, he eventually inherited his residence.
From that time on, he refined his practice and cultivated the subtle principles of ultimate truth. As his long-accumulated roots were profound, he experienced a sudden awakening and insight.

He then cast aside superficialities to investigate the fundamental depths, synthesizing various schools and reconciling differences to unify their ultimate aim. Thus, he weighed and balanced the teachings of the five periods.
Regarding the general outline of the ancestral vehicle of the single family of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, it is found within the *Zhiguan* (Cessation and Contemplation).

Therefore, what he harbored within was unfathomable, what he studied was inexhaustible, and his dialectical arguments were endless. Every time he took his seat to speak, his discourse reached its profound depths;

every example he cited was brilliant and radiant. Those who heard him could not help but be startled and moved, raising their voices to acclaim his excellence. Even the scholarly gentlemen of high standing [were impressed].

Scholars of elegant discourse sought him to discuss the Way through the night and throughout the day, yet none knew where he had gone. The Master waited for all beings with emptiness and embraced the multitude with compassion.

Those young men in their green collars flocked to his gate in eager haste, knocking to seek the Way as one looks toward clouds and rainbows during a great drought, or as an infant yearns for its mother’s milk—metaphors that fall short of describing him.
In his later years, he emerged from the mountains to propagate the transformation of beings.
To the east of Qiantang, the traditions of Chan and lecture-based study in Wu were quite flourishing;

some pursued the academic study of words and letters, while others indulged in the dissolute conduct of body and mouth, until these practices gradually became the prevailing custom—a state that had persisted for no small time.

Only our Master was able to resolutely rectify this collapsing order and extinguish its lingering embers. Among his disciples, many abandoned peripheral concerns to attend to the fundamental, turning from error toward the correct; thus it was. Therefore:
There were those who loathed and abandoned glory and honor; those who withdrew in seclusion after taking their leave; those who specialized in ritual recitation;

those whose only external possessions were robes and alms bowls; those who maintained themselves through the observance of fasts and precepts; those who engaged in lectures and discussions for the sake of universal salvation;

and those who found inner joy in meditative stillness—indeed, they were too numerous to count. Thus, that the transformative legacy of the former sages still endures in this final age is truly due to the efforts of these individuals.

He was promoted through successive appointments to prominent monasteries until his final residence at Nanping. When his karmic conditions were exhausted and his life’s work concluded, he manifested illness and passed away suddenly at the age of sixty-five and with fifty-four years of ordination. This was on the fifth day of the fourth month in the eighth year of the Xining era. His disciples interred his entire body to the right of the mountain and erected a stupa to mark it. In the eastern wing of the Heavenly Capital, he exerted himself through his reputation and deeds; having fulfilled his resolve for the Perfect Vehicle, he wondrously harmonized with the Imperial Ultimate.
That those of later generations have heard [the Dharma] is due to the power of this man.
At the Spirit Mountain in India, like-minded companions gathered like clouds; those who came did so with empty minds, while those who departed returned with full bellies.
The withered roots of the barren land are all moistened and nourished;
The western lake has its rear screen of peaks, and the stone chamber is filled with counting-sticks. The solitary moon suddenly falls, and the vast wilderness is doubly shrouded in darkness;
Only the pure breeze remains, spreading throughout the world.
Epitaph for the Great Master Tongyi of Xiangfu Temple On the tenth day of the eleventh month in the third year of the Yuanyou era, the Great Master passed away due to illness at his residence.
On the nineteenth day, he was cremated, and several hundred grains of blue-green *śarīra* were obtained. His disciples [enshrined them] on the twentieth day of the first month of the following year.

Six days later, his remaining bones were interred at the western foot of Lingyin Mountain. He had previously prepared a record of his life’s achievements and requested me to compose an inscription for his stupa;
unable to decline his request, I have thus composed this preface: The Great Master’s surname was阮 (Yuán), and his family had long been residents of Qiantang.

From his youth, he was exceptionally brilliant and did not delight in the mundane world. He left secular life to become a monk under the Venerable Zhāng of Xiángfú Monastery. There, he encountered the Heavenly... [text fragmentary].
Xipu’en (Xi Puren) was tonsured and received full ordination; his taboo name was Zining, his courtesy name Shijing, and his style name Chuanzhenzi.

Initially, he relied upon the Patriarch Yuyin to study the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the treatises of the Cien school. Subsequently, he followed Dharma Master Zishuan of Changshui to study the teachings and contemplations of the Xianshou school.

Thereafter, he returned to seclusion, burning dried wood and breaking off pine branches for fuel, while continuously lecturing and expounding upon such texts as the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* and the *Dharmapada*.
Whether it be the *Huayan*, the *Yuánjué*, or the *Jīngāng* [Sūtras], he lectured on them more than fifty times;

his practice possessed surplus vigor, and he extensively studied the works of Confucius, Zhou Gong, Laozi, Zhuangzi, and the various other schools, mastering their exegesis. He was skilled at composing literary prose and highly proficient in calligraphy.

He once composed the *Jīngāngxīn jīng kējì* (Outline Record of the Diamond Heart Sūtra) and a brief commentary on the *Cí'ēn Mítuó shū* (Ci'en’s Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra), each in one fascicle, which were published.

The *Song Gaoseng Zhuan Yin Yi* (Phonology and Meaning of the Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Song Dynasty) in three volumes; the *Cenxu Bensisi Tujing* (Revised and Continued Illustrated Scripture of One’s Own Temple) in one volume;

the *Xinxiu Guangyun Zilu* (Newly Compiled Character Register of the Expanded Rhyme Dictionary) in one volume; and miscellaneous writings including letters and commentaries totaling six volumes, along with over five hundred poems in both ancient and regulated verse styles.

His lifelong studies and exegeses were thus extensive; in his middle years, he retired from worldly affairs and spent four complete cycles reading the entire Tripitaka, including the Four Great Collections.

In one week, he traveled to several locations in Tokyo— including Fukan-ji, Chōkō-ji, Keisen-ji, and Unji-ji— where he personally collated and transcribed by hand over fifty fascicles of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and other scriptures from the Tripitaka.
Furthermore, he read two hundred copies of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, five hundred copies each of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*,

and the *Mahābodhicitta-uttaratantra-śrīmālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, as well as fifty thousand scrolls each of the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the *Amitābha-sūtra*, along with various secret mantras and sacred names.
His morning and evening recitations were beyond counting; his devotion to ascetic practice was as refined and thorough as this. A few days before his passing, he suddenly said to his disciples:
"My allotted lifespan is not long. After my death, you must not raise a funeral wail, change your mourning attire, or hold a night vigil for the bier.
However, someone may act on my behalf to compose a verse for my final moments and a letter of farewell."

He was frequently ridiculed by those who were knowledgeable [of the Dharma], as he lacked the ability to conform to worldly norms and brought shame upon me. Shortly thereafter, he lay ill and did not rise;

at the appointed time, he composed his mind, closed his eyes, counted his fingers, and passed away with serene composure. He was eighty-one years old in secular reckoning and sixty-nine in the monastic calendar.
He ordained the disciples Fan Lun, Fan Zhen, and Fan Ren, and his Dharma-grandsons were Si Zhen, Si Shou, Si Gong, and Si [Xun].
In sum, his lifespan ended in this manner. In the past, Baifa was preeminent for his virtue and deeds; his conduct in both movement and stillness served as a model for others.
The Great Master received and upheld his teachings, diligently following them in practice and exerting great effort in lecturing and recitation so as not to let their tradition decline.
Furthermore, in his leisure time, Baifa personally planted trees against a stone cliff beneath his courtyard to delight his eyes.

Regarding these amusements, the renowned worthies of the time all left behind their compositions. In his later years, the Great Master opened a window to cultivate flowers, continuing this personal interest;
moreover, he wished to never forget the legacy of his late teacher’s instructions throughout his life. Such was his reverence for the Way and his esteem for righteousness.

By nature, the Great Master was profound and resolute, acting without any levity. He lived in deep seclusion and quietude, finding contentment within himself, even though he was of noble lineage and high station.
He entered and exited their gates, yet never once bent even a foot of bamboo or compromised his Way to curry favor with the powerful and wealthy, nor did he seek fame or profit;

thus he nurtured his will and maintained his integrity. Although the Great Master’s learning was comprehensive and his virtuous achievements abundant, and his talent, eloquence, and calligraphy were preeminent among his contemporaries, he never boasted of his abilities or sought to extol his own virtues, nor did he rely on himself to look down upon others or criticize what they did not do.

To be short-sighted yet not to conceal the strengths of others; to be humble and modest, withdrawing from self-importance, being cautious in speech and sparing in error—such was his profound insight and far-reaching discernment.

Alas! Among men, there are those who live their entire lives without becoming scholars; those who study but do not apply themselves to cultivation; those who cultivate themselves but do not preserve righteousness;
those who possess righteousness but do not maintain integrity; and those who possess integrity but fail to honor their sense of duty. [He was the opposite of all these.]

There are those who possess these various virtues yet fail to reach their ultimate end; through this, we see that the Great Master, in his person and his Way, possessed both a beginning and a conclusion.
How could he have merely monopolized excellence for a single era? He shall also leave behind a legacy of abundance for future generations.
The inscription says:

The Hundred Dharmas and Five Teachings—nature and characteristics diverging; seeking them from all sides and lecturing upon them, one penetrates the profound and masters the subtle, thereby inheriting the legacy of the past.
Diligently cultivating one's virtue, maintaining integrity to the end, and acting without error, one perceives that empty flowers arise and perish, and the moon in water comes and goes;
yet only this remaining physical frame returns once more to the drifting dust.
To the west of Mount Ling, to the right of the Patriarch’s Stūpa, stones were piled and an inscription engraved to manifest [this record] for posterity.
This is the Epitaph for the Dharma Master Chao of Chaoguo in Huating.
The Dharma Master’s name was Lingzhao; his courtesy name was Liao Ran; his style was Xi-yi Zi. His father was of the Lu clan, originally from Lanxi in Dongyang.
The Dharma Master was born in the village of Jianye with extraordinary characteristics; he would not play with other children.
Having lost his parents, he resolved to escape the burdens of worldly life and informed his elder brother of this.

His brother wished to dissuade him, so he took three extremely coarse rattan whips and showed them to him, saying, "If I strike you and these rattan whips shatter, you may follow your own wishes. The Dharma Master joyfully leaped into the mountain forests.

He gathered some wisteria vines from nearby and, carrying them like a bundle of firewood to his elder brother, said, "Brother, if you truly intend to enter the Way, I shall strike you with this bundle of vines until they are all shattered;
even then, I shall have no regrets. His brother was moved to tears at once, realizing that his resolve could not be swayed.
He then had him take Shaoxian of Baohui Temple in the local county as his master. Upon entering the ranks of the monastic community, he vowed never again to use pillows or bedding.
He lit lamps and recited sutras day and night without ceasing; before long, he had mastered both the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Prabhāsa-sūtra*.

Having passed his early twenties, he brought his mastery of the scriptures to an examination and was immediately selected for the official quota. The local magistrate, admiring his keen intelligence, issued a special notice to honor him.
Upon shaving his head and receiving the full precepts, he maintained them with extreme rigor. He reflected privately: "If a person does not study, they will die in ignorance."
"A gentleman who has not heard the Way feels shame at this; how much more so for one who is a follower of the Buddha and takes the Way as his sole pursuit?

To eat to one’s fill and pass the time in vain, unaware of what is right—is this not lamentable? Thereupon, he set out in a boat across the river to Qiantang and stayed at the Xiangyan Hermitage, where he studied the Tiantai teachings under Dharma Master Zhan.
After serving him diligently for several years, he wished to seek further instruction elsewhere. The Master said to him, "You must not go anywhere else. This is the very place..."

Now, Dharma Master Jingjue is propagating the teachings in Wuxing; he is truly a peerless master of our school who appears once in an age. It is fitting that you go to him to rectify [your understanding].
Having received these instructions, the Master took his book-bag and traveled there. The bond between teacher and disciple was as harmonious as a needle meeting its eye;

they questioned each other deeply and reflected on the immediate, never flagging day or night. After several years, he attained thorough mastery of the doctrinal systems and contemplative practices of this school. Jingjue then desired—
Observing his capacity and magnanimity, he was tested with heavy responsibilities; the Dharma Master arranged matters according to circumstances, winning the hearts of the assembly.
When Jingjue passed away, the clergy and laity of Wuxing invited him to reside at Xiekong Monastery on Mount Wu. He subsequently moved to the Jietan Cloister at Jingde Monastery.
During the Xining era, Dharma Master Xiangyan resided at Chaoguo in Yunjian, where he exerted great effort to construct a center for Buddhist study until it was nearly complete.
When Beiwu was about to pass away, he entrusted his followers, saying: "I have exerted all my strength and dedicated my whole heart to establish this Dharma-center.
My constant wish is that someone who has received the true transmission of the teachings may succeed me; none other than Lingzhao can fulfill this.
Following these words, both the clergy and the laity conspired together to earnestly entreat the Master, who then led the assembly there. From far and near, people turned toward him with admiration.

His disciples flocked to him, practicing meditation and recitation with diligent austerity and preaching the Dharma without weariness. How much more so did they honor the teaching of the Pure Land and emulate the spirit of Donglin;
since the Yuanfeng era, they have formed a society of the fourfold assembly dedicated exclusively to Amitābha, vowing to depart for the Western Paradise.
Whenever the beginning of spring arrives, they initiate a Pure Land Dharma Assembly lasting seven days and nights, personally engaging in repentance with even greater intensity.
His cultivation reached such a state that over a period of two or three years, more than twenty thousand men and women joined the society;

the benefits they obtained and the miraculous responses they experienced were beyond counting. Once, while dreaming during his sleep, he beheld the extraordinary and sublime forms of Amitābha, Avalokiteśvara, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
The Dharma Master prostrated before them, knelt, and asked: "Lingzhao has spent her life reciting Mahāyāna sutras and studying the Mahāyāna Dharma."

Cultivating the practices of the Mahāyāna with the aspiration to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang) as his fruition, he asked Guanyin, who pointed and said, "The Pure Land is not far;
if you have the vow, you will be born there—do not doubt it again. Once, while reciting a sutra deep into the night, he leaned back and fell asleep.

Suddenly, in a dream, he saw the physical form of Samantabhadra, which filled him with joy. Startled awake, he immediately resolved to create an image of Samantabhadra and vowed to recite the *Dharmakṣānti-sūtra*.
He adorned the quarters with ten thousand varieties of flowers as a pure recompense for his remaining time, and his recitations and studies could not be fully recorded.
In the middle winter month of the fifth year of the Yuanfeng era, he suddenly lay ill and did not rise. Addressing his attendant, he said, "During my illness, I have witnessed extraordinary events;

the time for my rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang) is now certain. At dawn on the sixteenth day, with his head toward the north and his face toward the west, he placed his feet one upon the other and—

When his body grew cold after three days, his disciples followed the Western Indian custom of cremation. On that day, the heavens grew gloomy, the clouds mournful, the wind sorrowful, and the springs choked with grief;
white banners filled the four highways, and their wailing shook the great wilderness. The multitude piled fragrant wood and ignited it;
as the coffin opened and flames burst forth, some smelled a wondrous fragrance. When the smoke dispersed and the body was reduced to ash, [the relics remained].
Beholding this miraculous omen, his tongue-root remained unimpaired, supple and moist as if newly severed; fragments of *śarīra* (relics) streamed forth, alternating between red and white.
His lifelong achievements were thus made manifest. He was fifty-five years old by secular reckoning and thirty-four years since his ordination (*saṃgha-varṣa*).
More than a thousand people had come to his door to receive the Way, and those he personally ordained as disciples were named Jingren, Jueyuan, and Jingzhi. The following year...
On the eighteenth day of the middle winter month, his skeletal remains were interred in the southeast corner of the monastery, and a stupa was erected to mark the site.

The venerable Jingren repeatedly presented me with the monk’s life account and entreated me for a written commemoration. Having a long-standing friendship with the Dharma Master, I could not decline; thus, I have reluctantly composed this inscription, which concludes with these words: [The Inscription] follows.
The Dharma of India fanned the winds across Zhendan, and the Tiantai teachings flourished in Eastern Wu; those who truly bore this Way were indeed numerous.
How magnificent! The Master appeared as a model for the world, rescuing the lost youth and illuminating the dark alleys.

He pressed both precepts and meditation with equal urgency, aligning his conduct with his words. He gathered the Lotus Society to emulate the spirit of Mount Lu, diligently applying himself to dhyāna and recitation.
Ah! Following the footsteps of Great Su, the Way was sometimes obscured by the exigencies of the times; his physical form perished as it followed the transformations of things.
His *śarīra* rise like smoke, brilliant as clusters of pearls; his tongue-root remains amidst the flames, glowing like a red lotus.
The pillars and beams of the Dharma-gate are shattered, and the ferry-crossing for later students is lost. At Mount Ji and West Lake, in the eastern corner of Master Weng’s chamber, I behold this.
Who would not sigh with grief before his sacred tomb?
This is the Record of the Conduct and Deeds of Dharma Master Qingzhu of Qizhou during the Tang Dynasty.

The Dharma Master’s name was Huipu; he was the son of the Song family from Qishui in that same commandery. By nature, he was clear-sighted and lucid, and his capacity for understanding was transcendent.

Having received full ordination, Mei’s conduct was quite rigorous. At the beginning of the Yuanhe era, while traveling through Guangji County, he looked north for several li and saw peaks rising steeply and loftily like a screen. He then resolved to spend the rest of his life there;
with great enthusiasm, he took up his staff and ascended, finding a massive rock where he built a hut beneath it and vowed to recite the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* as his daily practice.
His mastery of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* had been cultivated over many years; he had thoroughly mastered the entire work, which consists of forty-two fascicles.
Some doubted its profundity and attempted to test him by randomly citing chapter titles, but the Master responded with a continuous flow of speech, entirely without hesitation or impediment.

Those who heard this could not help but marvel and submit, yet the Master paid them no mind, instead personally laboring at plowing and sowing to provide offerings for the morning meal, wearing only garments of grass and coarse cloth.

During the periods of the *fúlà* (the winter solstice and the new year), he remained in his usual practice, reciting the sutras morning and evening without slackening. His *bàn* (Sanskrit) voice was clear and resonant, echoing through the empty valleys.

Deep in the mountains and along secluded paths where human tracks were rarely seen, whenever a woodcutter passed by, he would always see a person in blue robes attending him, following him as he sat or rose.
From that time on, he abstained from grain and had no other concerns. Observers believed that there must have been some mysterious spirit making offerings to him.
Whenever anyone questioned him about his origins, the Master never spoke; thus, the local people marveled at his strangeness and named the mountain after his surname, Qing (Green).

In the tenth year [of the Kaiyuan era], his disciple Daojin organized a group of donors to establish the foundations and construct the buildings, founding a *saṃghārāma* and naming the monastery’s plaque after the mountain’s name.
On the twenty-seventh day of the tenth month of the twelfth year of the Dazhong era, he passed away with a serene countenance.
He quickly bathed, changed his robes, assembled the congregation to bid them farewell, sat cross-legged with his gaze withdrawn, and suddenly passed away.
His disciples wrapped his remains in fragrant clay, adorned them, and erected a stupa on the eastern peak of the monastery grounds.

At the beginning of the Imperial Dynasty, the third-generation descendant Deming, concerned that the site was perilous and inaccessible, making it difficult for people to ascend and descend, moved the monastery’s foundation to the foot of the mountain and relocated the stupa.

During the reign of Xining at the end of the Tang dynasty, his seventh-generation descendant, Zhihua, along with Zhitam, fearing that the temple and the pagoda were too distant for ritual services to be performed without interruption, moved the pagoda again to the northwest corner of the temple. They built an extension by the stream to connect it to the corridors and halls.
Up to the present, through eight generations and nearly two hundred years, the incense and lamps have never ceased. I have once perused the biographies of eminent monks of three successive dynasties.
Among the biographies, there is one section on the recitation of sutras that recounts many extraordinary events at the time of death.

Is this not because extensive learning and broad erudition do not compare to specializing in a single scripture? By fixing one's gaze upon the wondrous vehicle and refraining from engaging with worldly discourse, and by directing the mind toward the sacred realm to suddenly cease delusive conditions, one’s virtue moves the divine spirits while alive, and after death, the entire body remains indestructible, shaking the purity of the age.
I hope you will graciously provide a model for a thousand generations; how could this possibly be compared to those who rely on the light of a torch or flaunt the skills of a flying squirrel?

His grandson Zheyen once lamented that although his ancestors’ enduring excellence was recorded in various texts, these accounts were incomplete, erroneous, and insufficient to inspire confidence in the world.
Having traveled far to the region south of the Yangtze River, he repeatedly visited me.
Lu Jian, the Recorder, first ordered the compilation of these articles with the intention of carving them into stone to ensure their transmission for eternity.
Delighted by his keen intelligence, love of learning, filial remembrance of his ancestors, and reverence for virtue, I have edited and refined this work to satisfy his request.
The Record of the Venerable Master Donglin Chanhui’s Conduct and Virtues:
This master was the son of the Wu family of Donglin in Guian County, Huzhou; his name was Zhiyin and his courtesy name was Fuzhi.
From a young age, he grew weary of the mundane web of existence and aspired to transcendence. His parents marveled at this and permitted him to leave the household life when he was still but a youth.
For his capping ceremony, he took Zōjō of Jion-ji as his teacher. Before long, he had mastered the scriptural teachings; upon passing the examinations, he received ordination.
Subsequently, he ascended the dais to receive the precepts and intended to set out on travels for study, carrying his provisions and his book-satchel.

However, before long, his teacher grew old and died, so he succeeded him in his residence and did not fulfill his original ambition, which he always regretted. Nevertheless, whenever he encountered those who knew the Dharma and possessed the Way...

Those of noble character admired, envied, and respectfully submitted to him, rising from their seats to request instruction. Upon hearing even a single teaching, they received it with joy upon the crown of their heads, cherishing it reverently and never daring to forget it.
Consequently, they gained a general understanding of the Tripiṭaka—Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma—and the study of morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).

In his middle years, he heard the teachings and contemplations of the Pure Land, whereby he was certain to transcend all realms of existence and reach the state of non-retrogression. From that time forward, he devoted himself exclusively [to this practice].
He diligently performed rituals and recitations, concentrating his spirit and fixing his thoughts so that not a single day passed in vain. By nature, the Master was upright and honest;

he did not delight in clever speech, flattery, or assuming a fawning countenance to curry favor with others. Although he presided over various affairs, he was public-spirited, candid, and pure in his integrity, such that those above and below were both pleased and submissive.
He acted without pretense and spoke without levity. When interacting with monastics and laypeople alike, he addressed them solely by way of the principles of cause and effect and birth and death.
They exhorted one another, and consequently, the people of the neighborhood were moved by his example and followed his virtuous guidance.
In the autumn of the year when the reign title was changed to Yuánfú, he fell ill; he then withdrew from worldly affairs and ceased receiving visitors.

Though his body was frail and he struggled against his weakness, he did not lie upon a pillow or mat, but applied himself with even greater intensity to his daily recitations. One day, he said to his disciples, "I shall not rise again from this illness."
"I have vowed in my ordinary life to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing; now that time has arrived. Accordingly, he gathered the monks of the temple to assist him with Buddhist rites.
On the twenty-first day of the tenth month, at the hour of the Dragon (7–9 a.m.), the assembly of the temple gathered like clouds; they struck the sounding-stone and chanted the *Amitābha Sūtra*.

As they neared the end of the scroll, the Master sat cross-legged, closed his eyes, and passed away peacefully. After a night had passed, his countenance remained as if alive. His hometown was filled with grief.

When the laity heard of this, they hurried there carrying incense, prostrating themselves and offering praises beyond counting. He was sixty-nine years of age and had been a monk for forty-five years.
His disciples were named Shanqin, Youbang, and Sishang; all had departed elsewhere, leaving only Situan to attend to him during his illness until the end.
On the eleventh day of the second month of the following year, he was cremated according to the Indian method at [the location].
The śarīra were collected from the vicinity and interred in the rear garden of his original residence, where a stupa was erected to mark the site.
During the Yuanyou era, I once stayed at this temple for several nights while lodging in the Master’s quarters at the command of the *jie-jie* (boundary-delineation) ritual;

we spoke of the Master of Pure Practice (*jingye*), and he was quite sympathetic. Since then, we have been parted for over ten years, and as I have traveled between the north and south, I have almost entirely lost track of him.

Whether the Master was present or not, Bi Tan arrived and presented a detailed account of the Master’s life from beginning to end, bringing a formal biography (xingzhuang) with him and requesting a text as a commemorative record.
Moved by enduring feelings of remembrance, I have compiled this work;

furthermore, I wish to provide a witness to his life from start to finish to admonish my fellow practitioners, so that they may firmly resolve their will toward the West, no longer harboring self-doubt or self-obstruction that would lead to a deficiency in their spiritual aspiration.
This is sufficient.

The Śrāmaṇera Jiū of Xiangfu Temple in Hangzhou, whose courtesy name was Yilao and who was a son of the Qian family of Qiantang, grew weary of worldly life in his youth; he received ordination through the general amnesty of the Tiānshèng era.
Dù once studied the Tiantai teachings under Dharma Master Xiexi and delighted in composing ancient-style and regulated verse;

for the most part, his work reached a state of plainness and austere purity. Compared to other masters of the "clear and penetrating" or "obstructed and clogged" styles, he was neither superior nor inferior to them.

When Minister of the Left, Lord Pú, collected ancient and modern poetry from Qiántáng and sought the Master’s drafts, the Master said, "I take what I receive and immediately depart with it; I have never kept anything."
People also held him in high esteem; in his later years, he shut his door and cut off all visits, using the threshold as the boundary for receiving guests.
Even when the Inner Secretary Su Gong and Lin Gong of Koudi—both eminent men of their time—met him on the road and came to visit, he never once condescended to see them.
When I first heard of this, I composed a poem in jest: "Break and snap the old cane staff at the head of the bed; Let the peach and plum trees do as they please."
"How was it that in the past, Mount Lu was so remote that even Tao Qian had to cross its stream? The Master smiled but did not answer.
His quarters were dilapidated and humble, such that others could not bear the distress; beneath his courtyard grew only a few stalks of red banana and several hundred bamboos.

He called this place the "Tiao-tiao Hall" (Hall of Whistling), and while residing there, he moved with ease whether walking in meditation or sitting in repose. When he fell ill and was about to pass away:
He would often say to people, "When I die, the banana and bamboo will also die; Master Zeying will also die.
At that time, Master Ying was still in good health, yet later all his words came true. No one could fathom him. As he was about to depart, he composed a verse extemporaneously, saying:

"Birth, old age, sickness, and death—joy lies within them. That is all! Deliver this message to the wind, flowers, snow, and moon. Having finished speaking, he passed away at the age of [blank] years.
The eighty disciples buried his bones at a Chan monastery on North Mountain. I have always held him in deep respect;
whenever I passed his former residence, I was moved by a sense of sorrow. Therefore, I shall set forth several matters here to serve as an instruction for those who come after.
The Record of the Deeds of Dharma Master Weizhan of Chaoguo in Xiuzhou.
The Master was originally a son of the Song family of Yiwu in Dongyang; Weizhan was his name, and Zizhao was his courtesy name.
On the day before he was born, a monk of divine异象 (extraordinary appearance) said to his father: "You shall have six sons, and the fifth..."
"You must be careful not to detain him; he should be permitted to leave the household life, for he will surely propagate the Great Teaching.

During the Xiangfu era, his mother, Lady Chen, gave birth to the Dharma Master. When he was still a child, he conceived the desire to renounce the world, but his parents opposed him, which caused him to fall ill.
Only then did his father realize the words of the extraordinary monk from the past and thus grant his wish. He subsequently took Huíqín of Shānglín Monastery as his teacher.

The temple was the very residence of the Great Being (Mahāsattva) of the Liang dynasty. During the Tianxi era of the Zhenzong reign, Fashi received the tonsure and ordination as part of a universal ordination of monks and nuns throughout the land.
The following year, he received full ordination and strictly observed the traditional monastic precepts.

Deeply delighting in the Perfect Vehicle (Paryanta-yāna), he heard that the teachings of Tiantai were flourishing greatly in Jiangzuo; he subsequently went to Tiantai to seek out Shenzhao of Dongye Mountain.
He sought instruction from the Dharma Master; by day he investigated the subtle meanings, and by evening he performed repentance rituals.
With his three karmas applied with such diligence that not even a moment was wasted, his fellow students came to call him "Dao-ren" (The Wayman).

He further visited the gate of Guangzhi at Siming, seeking out diverse teachings and extensively researching their refined principles. Having sat there for ten years and achieved great success, he remarked: "The Great Master’s..."

Having attained [the Way] himself, he also caused others to attain it; he subsequently ascended the hall to seek further instruction, vigorously expounding the Dharma for the assembly, such that those from all quarters looked toward him with admiration and the multitude of students submitted in awe.
He then reflected to himself: "I no longer harbor any doubts regarding what the Great Master has bestowed upon me.

However, as for the ultimate principle of the Perfect and Sudden teaching that is free from all relativity, unless I have attained it through profound cultivation and self-realization, I dare not presume to claim mastery myself. Thus, he cultivated his mind with patience and gentleness, accumulating [his practice].
As he contemplated this, he suddenly attained a vast and clear realization beneath the words of the Patriarch, his doubts dissolving like ice melting away.
He then engaged in discussion with his fellow students and senior practitioners; some bowed their heads in submission, while others rolled up their sleeves in defiance.
The Dharma Master sighed deeply and said: "The Way of our Buddha is called 'Non-contention' (araṇā) by those who have realized it."

Since even the state of non-delusion is beyond the reach of speech and thought, how could it tolerate frivolous conceptualization? He thereupon rolled up his robes and returned to his hometown, settling once more in his former hermitage.
There he burned cypress wood to offer incense to the moon, far continuing the tradition of Dazhu Huihai; he lived on vegetarian fare and water, loftily emulating the discipline of Zhizhe of Chicheng.

Finding joy in seclusion within the forests and fields, he devoted himself to meditation and recitation. After some time, he reflected: "My ancestors have taught that propagating the Dharma is [the primary duty]."
"I must not become one who severs the lineage of the Buddhas at its end; how could I now pursue only my own private perfection? Is this not a failure of foresight for my descendants?
Thinking thus, he took up his staff and came to Wu, where he established the Jingsha (Crimson Silk) Hall at the Xiangyan Hermitage in Qiantang.

He subsequently moved to Dongyue and later resided at Yunchuan, which was the Chaoguo Monastery. As soon as the Dharma Master arrived, the common people and officials bowed like grass before the wind, and the assembly of students gathered around him.

When the assembly gathered, he would occasionally unfurl the scrolls of the *śāstras* and wield the handle of his eloquent discourse; his profound and resonant voice struck awe into the ears of the multitude.

Whether ascending to the hall or entering the inner chambers, wherever the rain of the Dharma fell, all were moistened and benefited. Beyond his lectures and exegesis, his heart was set upon the promotion of the faith;
he exhorted the noble clans to diligently cultivate meritorious works, commissioning carvings of the Holy Image of Amitābha and opening halls for the *Sukhāvatī-vyūha* repentance rites.
The lecture hall, the abbot’s quarters, and all the surrounding buildings and necessary implements for ritual service were entirely renovated.

From this point on, it was through the Master that the Way of Tiantai and the teachings of the Pure Land began to spread throughout Zhongwu. The mountain school’s contemplative practices and the various volumes of the Mahayana and Hinayana canons were expounded in continuous cycles;
these cannot be recorded in full detail. This [stele] was erected on the eighth day of the third month in the sixth year of the Xining era.
When the seven-day period of the *Guangming Chanhui* (Light-Brilliance Repentance Assembly) had concluded and the assembly was about to disperse, he summoned his disciples and suddenly declared:
"My karmic conditions for this life have reached their limit; I wish to take my leave of you all. You must listen to my words.

He then recited passages from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Yijiao jing* (Sutra on the Bequeathed Teachings), earnestly entrusting them with his final instructions. His words were so piteous that the entire assembly shed tears as they spoke.
He passed away while sitting upright in the full lotus posture. On another day, his body was cremated, and several hundred grains of *śarīra* were obtained, brilliant as pearls.

When subjected to the fire of smelting iron or struck with metal hammers, they remained unbroken with a resonant *keng* sound. Were it not for the power of precepts, concentration, and wisdom, how could such a thing have occurred?
His disciples constructed a stupa from the remaining bones at Huiriyuan on Yushan to the west of the county seat. He was sixty-five years old at the time of his death. The monk [passed away].
In his fifty-third year, he personally ordained disciples named Zhitong, Zongyong, Zongshe, and Zonggu;
those who entered his gate to receive the Dharma were beyond counting. Master Haihui Yuan was truly a preeminent senior disciple who attained the Dharma.
One day, [a disciple] described his deeds and virtues and requested a preface from me. Unable to refuse, I have therefore compiled and arranged this account, hoping it may be of some benefit.
According to the *Sengshi* (History of the Sangha), it records the biography of Dharma Master Guangci of Leifeng Peak in Hangzhou.
The master’s name was Huicai, with the style name Tanyuan; he was the son of the Wang family of Yueqing, Yongjia. From his youth, he possessed extraordinary character and delighted in...
Having grown weary of the secular world for five years, he entered Baihe Temple in his native district to take Yi-fang as his preceptor.
Encountering the grace of the Xiangfu amnesty, he received the tonsure at thirteen and subsequently received full ordination.

Hearing that the Dharma seat of the Tiantai school’s teachings and doctrines was flourishing under the Great Master Fazhi of Siming, he went there to study; however, because his natural endowment was dull and he was at a loss for what to do, he said: "I..."

Having heard that the Great Being Avalokiteśvara’s vast vows benefit all beings and that he surely responds to those who seek him, I shall now maintain the name of Avalokiteśvara and recite the Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī, hoping thereby for my mind and wisdom to become clear and for my learning to penetrate the ancestral teachings.
One night, as if in a dream, I saw a Brahman monk several zhang tall who called out my name; he then took off the *kāṣāya* he was wearing and bestowed it upon me to wear.
He entrusted him with the words, "Throughout your life, keep me in mind; I shall assist you. The following day, he attended a lecture assembly and attained sudden, vast enlightenment.
What he saw with his eyes and heard with his ears was as if it were long-practiced habit; everything he had previously heard was now thoroughly understood.

His peers were struck with wonder, crowding shoulder to shoulder to consult and question him. His responses were unimpeded. Thereupon, Fazhi commanded him to lead the assembly in the recitation of the scriptures.

Whenever he was requested to explain the meaning of the teachings, students would gather around him like a circle. Fazhi (Dharmajñāna) would frequently praise their attainments before the assembly, and from this, his reputation spread in all directions.
His seniors deferred to him, and later he went to the seat of Master Ciyun at Tiantong in Qiantang, where he served under him as a disciple.
There, he gained even more extraordinary insights. Subsequently, as his understanding and practice reached maturity, scholars flocked to him in numbers like ants.
At Baoshan Guangyan Monastery, he led his disciples in lecturing for three years; then he moved to Zhuge on Mount Gu for another three years;
and after twenty-odd years at Nanshan Fohui Temple, he was invited by Lord Zhi Mao to reside at Fushiyuan in Quzhou.
At the beginning of the Zhiping era, Prefect Shen invited him to return and reside at Fahui Baoge, where Grand Marshal Lu submitted a memorial on his behalf.

The master was titled Guangci (Extensive Compassion). In his old age, he sought to retire from his post; the people of Hangzhou lamented his departure and built a hermitage for him at Leifeng on South Mountain.

He lived to the age of eighty-six, with seventy-three years of ordination. The number of times he lectured on sutras and śāstras, as well as the number of people he ordained for the sake of the assembly, is beyond counting.

His miraculous responses and deeds are omitted here to avoid prolixity. Throughout his life, the master relied primarily upon the *Mahākaruṇā-mantra* as his spiritual practice, achieving results with little effort.
At that time, he would often remain in the *utkuṭaka* posture (kneeling with the heels together) for an entire day, reciting [the scriptures] without showing any sign of weariness.

Thereafter, he made it his practice to maintain this posture for a period of one hundred and eight repetitions at each session. Furthermore, desiring to vow rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*), he would recite the name of Amitābha while kneeling for a full day and night;
his utmost sincerity was always of this nature. As his end approached, he received a miraculous dream and said, "My rebirth in the Pure Land is certain. He then changed his robes and rose.
Having finished writing these verses in praise of the Buddha while seated, he passed away peacefully on the twenty-first day of the fifth month in the sixth year of the Yuanfeng era.
On the tenth day of the intercalary sixth month of that same year, his disciples enshrined his whole body to the right of the hermitage and erected a stupa to commemorate him.
By nature the Master was serene and his appearance ancient; he spoke little, had few desires, and his deportment was grave and dignified as he interacted with others.
The various masters of the Tiantai teaching tradition held differing opinions, and as teacher and disciple clashed, their disputes caused a great stir throughout Jiangzhe.
Yet the Master exhausted all that he knew to instruct his disciples with steady persistence; whether matters were good or bad, long or short, he never allowed them to take form in his speech.
Noble yet not aloof, harmonious yet not drifting, he spent over forty years coming and going in Qiantang, never associating with the secular world, while leading assemblies wherever he stayed.

Provisions were supplied for his service, and high officials and scholars held him in awe and reverence; they venerated his lofty character and followed his lead, all arriving spontaneously without prior consultation.
Were it not for the possession of both merit and wisdom, how could one reach such a state? In his daily life, he partook of the two meals—morning and evening—and engaged in teaching and recitation;
even when ill, he never failed to join the assembly. When he grew old, he entered a hermitage and never emerged again for the rest of his life, despite the presence of those with power and influence.
In the end, Shi was unable to humble him; he was truly a high monk of his generation.

Those who came to his gate to receive the Way were beyond counting, yet those whom he personally ordained as disciples numbered ten. Among them, Fazong one day itemized these matters and requested a commemorative text from me.
Having previously received the precepts from the Master and thus knowing him quite thoroughly, I have therefore compiled and arranged this account to serve as a record for future generations.
The biographer relates:
Dharma Master Ying of Xiangfu Temple in Hangzhou has a bone-stupa inscription.
The Master’s name was Zheyiṅ, his style name was Yùnzhī, and he was the son of Yu of Tóngjiāng. His mother, Lady Wáng, once dreamed of two suns appearing together...

She took advantage of the occasion to meet him and they became intimate; consequently, she conceived. Suspecting she would surely give birth to two sons, she waited until the months were complete, but gave birth to only one son.
In the following year, she conceived again and produced another son, which finally corresponded to her dream of two days.
Her parents marveled at this and allowed both to leave the household life; each attained ordination through their mastery of the scriptures. Both were exceptionally bright and keen in their studies.
The student was a man of high character and integrity. His eldest son, named Ziqin (字: Xigu), studied under the master at Jingzhu Monastery in Qiantang;
he later traveled abroad for study and passed away on Mount Tiantai. The second son was the Dharma Master himself.

Having lost his mother while still young, he followed his father to Hangzhou, where he first donned the white robes [of a layperson] at Rui峰 (Rui Peak) on South Mountain. Subsequently, he took refuge with Master Chubang of Shouning Monastery.
Having become a teacher, he was already endowed with the foremost precepts; his reputation for excellence in studying the Vinaya had already surpassed his contemporaries.
Because he was a novice, the teacher also harbored some self-conceit. During the Xining era, Dharma Master Shenwu of Dongye Mountain came to reside at Baojue Temple.

When the teacher went to see him, he was struck with awe and filled with shame upon hearing the Master’s exposition, whereupon he said: "I did not expect that in this degenerate age there would again be..."

"This man is truly my teacher; it would have been a great misfortune had I not met him. Thereupon, with a humble mind and purified self, he served as his disciple, facing north, drawing back his robes to show respect, and requesting instruction morning and evening without slackening.

His spiritual realization was such that the Master also held him in high esteem. Although the Master had extensively studied the sutras and śāstras, he found particular inspiration in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Consequently, while reading the *Fahua wenju* (The Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra) and the *Jingang bei* (The Diamond Scalpel), he remained awake for several nights.
The Moon then reported what he had attained to his teacher. The teacher said, "The sublime purport of the Lotus Sūtra returns to one's own self;
you should protect and uphold it well, and never disparage yourself. I only fear that if a mani jewel of supreme value is cast into a worn-out sack, it will not be a fitting place for it.

From that time on, his learning and conduct became renowned, and like-minded friends looked toward him with admiration; it was as if a mirror, when cleansed of dust, reflects images, or as a bell [resounds when struck].
With an inner void, he responds to every strike; as for his Way, it is neither fettered by forms nor distracted by emptiness.
As for his character, he does not cling to the times nor stagnate in material things. His speech is without artifice, and his conduct is without sycophancy.

Whether migrating between north and south, he labors for the sake of the Dharma; whether walking or staying, he follows conditions; whether departing or remaining, the initiative rests with him. Thus, he may lead a community and serve as abbot.
He traveled to lecture while residing in various places such as Suzhou, Hangzhou, Lake District, and Xiuzhou, visiting more than twenty locations.

In his middle years, he suffered frequently from illness and consequently settled at the ancient monastery of Xiangfu. There, he wielded his whisk with such vigor that monks and scholars gathered like clouds;

his deep voice and rapid eloquence caused all who heard him to stand with ears pricked and eyes wide in admiration, marveling at his extraordinary brilliance. In the spring of the second year of the Yuanfu era, he fell ill, and medicine could not cure him. As he approached his end...
He performed self-reflection, saying: "For twenty years I have exclusively propagated the Supreme Vehicle to awaken the masses;
how could it be that I am now beset by this illness and suffering, unable to overcome it? Is it not because what I have transmitted has failed to accord with the intent of the Sage?

He then took his lifelong writings and burned them before the assembly. Rising with vigor, he faced west, leaned upon a desk, and commanded the assembly to recite the *Amitābha Sūtra*. No sooner had he begun...
The transmission of his teachings suddenly ceased on the twenty-ninth day of the third month; he was fifty-five years old and had been a monk for thirty-two years.
Five days later, his cremation took place in the wilds of Xiàhú. On that day, white banners filled the roads and piles of fragrant wood were stacked high.
Laypeople and monastics followed him for several li, such that the carriage tracks and horse paths could not accommodate them. When the fire was extinguished, his remains were found scattered.

Some said that while the Dharma Master had been of great benefit to the world, his passing into stillness meant that his enduring influence and sublime legacy would soon vanish without a trace—a prospect our community could not bear.
We therefore sent someone to filter the water, recovering about half of his remains;
we erected a stupa and buried them to the west of the Lotus Pond in the Repentance Hall at Lingzhi. I was requested to compose an inscription for it. I have known this Master since childhood.

Having been companions since childhood until we sat for the same scriptural examinations and studied together under the same teacher, I am well aware of his extensive learning and thus did not dare decline.
The inscription reads:
The Supreme Sage descended as a spirit, solely for the sake of the One Reality; On Vulture Peak he opened the provisional gates, and in the Crane Forest he upheld the Vinaya.
Tiantai attained wondrous enlightenment, and Zhang’an followed his legacy; were it not for Master Fabao, who could have plumbed its profound and subtle depths?

He distinguished between what was virtuous and what was not, and rectified its strengths and weaknesses. Some dwell in existence while others sink into emptiness—like those with tiger skins but sheep’s natures.
As for those who merge with the Truth, they neither stir nor emerge; as for those bound by numerical conditions, they have a beginning and an end.
Gathering his seeds, he leaned upon his desk; In full lotus posture, he withdrew into his chamber. The incense has long since burned out, yet his presence remains;

His relics are enshrined within a stupa. Lotuses bloom and wither; The lake’s light appears and disappears. He leaves this behind as a teaching for all disciples— How can one ever finish gazing up toward him?
Epitaph for the Stupa of the Venerable Master Yi of Yuyao, Yue State.
Shi Danyizi Yinzhī was the son of the Du family of Yuyao, Yuezhou. While still a youth with his hair tied in two tufts (*guanjiao*), he already possessed an extraordinary ambition.
He left secular life at Longquan Temple to take Qingxu as his preceptor; having received the imperial amnesty of the Huangyou era, he obtained the tonsure.
Once he had completed the full precepts, he carried his book-box and bundle and studied the Tiantai teachings under Master Yun of Siming. From him...
Later, he traveled extensively throughout all directions, where he came to know the new and refresh his knowledge of the old.

He entered the gates and became disciples of Tianzhu Mingzhi, Leifeng Guangci, and others, diligently seeking instruction for over twenty years. Once his studies were complete, he returned to his former seclusion.
Although monastics and laypeople urged him to take up the position of abbot, he resolutely refused to accept. Alas, as the elders pressed him earnestly, he could not but comply.
Having thus delivered lectures on the Perfect Vehicle (Yuan-sheng) at his original temple, his audience was moved to joyful submission.

In his later years, he declined social affairs, closed his door and did not go out, strictly arranging a single room to specialize in the practice of Pure Land. He worshipped the Buddha and recited the sutras without ceasing day or night.
In the first year of the Chongning era, as the summer retreat was about to end, he suddenly fell slightly ill. On the nineteenth day, he summoned his disciples and burned [incense].
Xiang told him, "The time for me to be born in the Pure Land has arrived. I shall mount the Vajra-pedestal and follow the Buddha westward;
