Alas for my deceased parents! Their accumulated deeds are worthy of record, yet that future generations may not hear of them is a source of shame for a filial son.
Reflecting upon this upbringing, they were truly my pillars and my reliance; their virtue was inexhaustible, and how could their heart have its end?
Who is there who, as a younger brother, serves his elder brother as he would a father? Who is there who, as a wife, serves her husband as she would a lord?
In life, we shall grow old together; in death, we share the same earth. This inscription is engraved upon the dark spring to illuminate eternity.
Epitaph for the Tomb of Master Left (Zuo Jun) of Taizhou:

The Master’s name was Shen, with the courtesy name Junyi. His family had been natives of Linhai for generations. He was humble and respectful, upright and straightforward, simple and easygoing, and tranquil in his conduct.

He did not walk with haste and spoke without frivolity. In managing his household and conducting his livelihood, he never exploited others for even a hair’s breadth of profit through unrighteous means.

When offended by others, he never showed it in his countenance; when hearing of another's faults, he never mentioned them. Knowing of the virtues of others, he revered and admired them as if he could not keep up with them.
By nature, he delighted in Buddhist principles; whenever he encountered followers of the Buddha, regardless of whether they were worthy or unworthy, he treated them all with utmost sincerity.
Truly devoted to the practice of propriety, while still in the prime of his youth, he sought the Bodhisattva precepts from Dharma Master Shenzhao of Mount Dongye.
The Dharma Master praised him before the assembly, stroked his head, and bestowed a prophetic record upon him. From that time forth, he strictly observed the pure prohibitions;

on every fast day, with the exception of the midday meal, he would not take into his mouth any food or medicinal decoctions containing form. Once, when a banquet was being held for his relatives, they invited him to join them.
Although he was urged with bitter and earnest words, he ultimately would not yield, saying, "How could I comply with human whims and deceive the Buddha’s regulations?
Thus, for forty years until his death, he did not alter [his practice]. He carved images of the Three Sages of the West without haggling with the artisan over their price;
he recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* more than three thousand four hundred times and the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* more than twenty thousand times; and he built bridges.
He repaired roads and provided relief to the orphaned and destitute, sparing nothing in his generosity. He married Huang of Dadian, who was gentle, virtuous, and possessed noble conduct;
she also inclined toward Buddhism. They had six sons: Taiwei, who pursued the Confucian path and achieved renown in the examination halls;
Liangwang, who was filial, fraternal, and broadly affectionate, yet unfortunately died young; Taiyi; Wan; Jiao; one who became a Buddhist monk; and Jing.
The three daughters of Yuan married into the Huang family; after they passed away, he did not marry again.

He lived alone at a separate estate on Mount Dong, where, beyond his daily rites and recitations, he would sit all day long with his legs crossed and leaning against a desk, appearing composed and serene.
Someone said to him, "Is your dwelling not rather desolate? The Master replied, "According to the Buddhist scriptures, there is a Buddha hall and a Buddha image here; how could it be desolate?"
One day, while Liaozhi was passing by his desk, a swallow wished to nest upon it. The Master said, "If you nest here, I fear it will defile my scriptures.
After a short while, the swallow moved elsewhere. Such was his power in moving things. In the autumn of the second year of the Shaosheng era, he lay ill and did not rise.

He instructed the monks to perform morning and evening repentances and recitations. Despite his illness, the Master forced himself to rise and chanted the Buddha’s name with a resolute voice until the end.
Having already prepared his hands and feet for the journey, he purified himself and recited the opening title of the *Lotus Sūtra* while increasing his bodhisattva precepts.
He then dreamed of three great figures whose countenances were brilliant and pure, standing upon the riverbank; they summoned him to board their boat and vanished instantly as they headed westward.
He took this to be the preliminary guidance of the Three Sages, and from then on, he gave away all his cherished possessions, distributing them among those both old and young.
He urgently summoned a monk to recite the *Amitābha Sūtra*. Before it was finished, he said, "I have already attained realization;
my rebirth in the Pure Land is certain. An attendant asked, "What is this realization? He replied, "I have already received the Buddha’s light.

He then bathed, changed his robes, and dismissed those around him with a stern command not to weep, fearing it would disturb his mind. Reciting the Buddha's name and forming mudrās, he passed away in profound stillness. This indeed happened.
It was the twelfth day of the ninth month of that year. He reached the age of seventy-two.
His orphans selected a certain month and day of the following year to bury him at Zifangyao in Jiangnan, in accordance with the rites.

During the Yuanyou era, I once resided in Taicheng, where I frequently visited the descendants of the Zuo family and the Jingyuan Monastery; as I knew the Master well, I subsequently traveled across the streams and mountains there.
He has come from more than a thousand *li* away, desiring to request an inscription to commemorate his tomb; unable to decline his request, I have recorded the facts with a straightforward pen.
As for investigating the origins of his lineage or composing elegant and ornate prose, I am not equal to the veteran scholars.
The inscription reads: [The Inscription] says: [Insert text here].
Alas! Your demeanor was noble; your nature was perfected by Heaven. You dwelt in reverence and acted with simplicity, keeping away what is depraved and preserving sincerity.
By observing what you cultivated, we see that you were long-lived and at peace; by examining your end, the proof becomes clear.
Those who scheme for life do not meet their natural death, while those who understand death alone preserve their true life.
"You are indeed complete [in virtue]. How could I dare not inscribe this?
This is the epitaph for the tomb of Lord Yao of Xinsi.
A son of the Yao clan, having lost his father three years ago, one day wept and informed me, saying: 'My late lord, by..."
On the seventeenth night of the tenth month in the first year of the Yuanyou era, he passed away at his residence at the age of seventy-five.
He was married to Shen Meilin and had two sons, namely Ming and his younger brother Shi. There were six grandsons: Jian, Chong, Cheng, Yuan, Jia, and Yuan.
On the twenty-third day of the third month this year, his remains were cremated according to the Western Dharma; the funeral took place on the twenty-fifth day.
To bury the remaining bones in the cemetery of my grandmother was the lifelong wish of my late father.

I reflect that when parents possess virtue yet their children cannot live up to it, according to the rites, this is called unfiliality; furthermore, throughout his life, my late father practiced goodness only the Master truly knows.
I pray that you will compose an inscription for his tomb so that his legacy shall not fall into oblivion. I grieve for his loss and cherish the memory of his father’s—
For the sake of others, I have composed this preface: The Master’s name was Ying; his family had resided for generations in Xinshi Town, Deqing County, Huzhou.

His ancestors were of humble means, yet they exerted their utmost strength to serve their parents, maintaining integrity in their conduct and practicing frugality to expand their enterprise until they became a prominent clan.

Upon the death of his father, he honored the father’s final instructions and transformed himself accordingly; when his mother passed away, his grief and longing remained unceasing, and he subsequently interred her.
In the gardens near his residence, he constructed a pavilion where he dwelt for the rest of his life. From year to year, he performed memorial services to repay the boundless kindness of his parents;

whenever anyone mentioned them, his tears would flow incessantly. Such was his pure filial piety. In his middle years, he entrusted the affairs of the household to his son and lived in quiet seclusion to nourish his will.
He read Buddhist scriptures, recited the Buddha’s name, and observed the six fast days and the five precepts until the end of his life.
In his old age, he made it his constant practice to venerate stupas and images, repair monasteries, provide offerings to the saints, and feed the monks;
these acts were beyond counting. During severe winters and years of famine, he provided relief to the orphaned and the destitute.

Furthermore, regarding the construction of bridges and the digging of public wells—whatever was beneficial to others—he took the initiative to perform such deeds, contributing his wealth and silk as if he had no concern for them. Such was Shen’s delight in giving.

Having lost his wife, he vowed never to remarry and lived alone as a widower, yet he remained serene and content. Although his close relatives earnestly urged him to change, they could never turn his resolve;
he said, "How could I indulge my own private desires and bring calamity upon my descendants? Such was his purity and prudence:
whenever he approached his meals at dawn or dusk, he would invariably repeat the act three times while kneeling with clasped hands, offering thanks and repentance to Heaven. Furthermore—
He caused his entire family to follow his example; although he was wealthy, he always acted as if he were lacking, frequently saying to others, "My family rose from humble origins;
though our wealth and food are now sufficient, I dare not forget our beginnings.
In his later years, when his clan had flourished, his residence remained modest. His son then selected timber to expand the mansion, yet the Master would never [consent].

Lè said, "To me, this is utterly beyond my station. He maintained himself in such a manner that, although he was a patriarch of the village, he never relied on his own status to treat others with contempt;
even toward those who were cold or lowly, he spoke with a warm countenance as if there were no distinction between high and low.
Therefore, when he stayed at home, even his servants and slaves loved him; when he went out, even the strong and headstrong feared him. Among the neighbors, there were some who...
Regarding matters of contention that seem almost impossible to resolve, one must seek counsel from you; when you go and speak but a single word, they are invariably pacified and submit.
His clothing and possessions were like this. Several months before his death, he suddenly had many straw mats prepared.

When asked the reason for this, he said, "I shall not remain long; I have certainly commanded Buddhist practitioners to perform liturgical recitations to serve as my funeral bedding," out of respect for them.
He was pure and meticulous, and further instructed his son, saying: "After my death, you should perform meritorious deeds to assist me in attaining rebirth;

as for other matters that yield no benefit, though they may be esteemed by the ancients and the moderns alike, be careful not to engage in them. At first, people did not believe him, but when the appointed time arrived, it turned out exactly as he had said.
Such was his manner of passing away. Indeed, pure filial piety is benevolence (*ren*); delighting in giving is righteousness (*yi*); and purity and caution are propriety (*li*).

To preserve one's own wisdom is integrity; to serve all things with sincerity is trustworthiness. These are the means by which one brings one's life to a successful conclusion. Moreover, if a person possesses even a single virtue, it is sufficient to praise them;
how much more so when they are endowed with these several qualities—how could one fail to commemorate them? The inscription reads: [The Inscription] says: [Insert the specific inscription here].
How sublime are the Five Constant Virtues! They are the very nature of Heaven and originally so. The myriad people are ignorant and simple;
when they are instructed in these principles and possess even one of them, they become gentlemen. How much more so for such a person as this, who is fully endowed with all these beauties!
Though the physical form may perish, virtue does not die. May his plans for descendants be perpetually bestowed, providing a model for a hundred generations.
Epitaph for the Tomb of Mr. Shen of Xiuzhou.
His name was Yanlu; his family had been residents of Jiaxing for generations, originally from the Baimu (White Hemp) Township.

Later they moved to the city of the prefecture, and not long after, they selected another residence elsewhere, donating their former estate to serve as the monastery quarters for Benjue Temple. As a man, he was dignified and generous, possessing great virtue from his youth.
Xiaoke succeeded to his family estate as if he were already a mature adult. He served his parents with filial piety and governed his household according to ritual propriety;
he remained unchanging in his self-discipline and refrained from competing with others. Consequently, he was praised by the virtuous among his fellow villagers.
In all matters, he invariably offered his sincere devotion to the Buddha, focusing his attention especially on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, for which he commissioned monks to recite it.

He never ceased for a year’s time his constant practice of maintaining the secret mantra for the elimination of calamities through Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). He made offerings to the holy ones and provided meals for the Sangha in incalculable numbers.
On the twenty-sixth day of the tenth month in the fourth year of the Yuanfeng era, he fell ill and passed away at his residence at the age of seventy-nine.
His first wife was Lady Zhou, who died earlier; he later married Lady Ding. Their eldest son was named Wenya, followed by...
It is said that Wen-yi’s two daughters both married into other clans; her grandsons are named Zongdao, Zongqie, and Zongmin, who have followed the teachings of the Śākya clan;
and her three granddaughters are still unmarried. On the twenty-second day of the third month of the sixth year, they were about to undergo cremation.
Because I was attending a Dharma assembly, I passed through Xiucheng, where the bereaved family recorded these details and requested my assistance. I complied with their request.
I inscribe this, grieving that he has passed away; though I decline, I cannot avoid it. The inscription says:
Through righteousness one attains wealth; through benevolence one attains longevity. His beginnings were already renowned; his end is even more flourishing.
He accumulated goodness in his present life; his remaining blessings shall extend to posterity.
Epitaph for the Tomb of Lord Lü Chongde:
Zhongdan was his courtesy name, and Zihou was his style name. His family had resided [there] for generations. During the time when the State of Qi ruled, his distant ancestors all held office;
however, after the territory was surrendered and they returned to the fields, there were no further successors. Xingchen was his great-great-grandfather, and Rencong was his grandfather.
Zu was his grandfather and Wen-huang his father. From childhood, Jun was orphaned, yet he was able to manage the household; by the time he reached adulthood, the family estate had flourished.
He first married into the Chen family, who bore him two sons—Zonggu, who died young, and Zongyan, who succeeded to his father’s legacy—and one daughter, who married Jiang Fang, a local resident.
He had five grandsons: Jing, Kang, Yong, and Heng, while the fifth followed [his lineage].
The Shi clan says that Huizi was his great-great-grandson, and there were fourteen great-great-great-grandsons; in one generation, more than fifty members of the family lived together.

Thus, throughout five generations, the Master saw them all. He married last into the Liu family, who passed away before him. The Master’s natural endowment was profound and grave, and his appearance was imposing;
he looked formidable from afar, yet he was warm and respectful toward others and free from contention. In middle age, he suffered from illness.
His hearing and sight became dull and obstructed, so he sought repentance from the Buddha and reverently maintained their esoteric teachings; before long, he was suddenly cured.

From then on, he declined all social affairs and remained secluded within his gate for nearly thirty years. His descendants were all filial and respectful, providing him with constant care and support.
Although his family was wealthy and noble, he was humble and frugal, always appearing as if he lacked enough whenever it came to food and clothing.
He would invariably clasp his hands in a gesture of apology and thanksgiving before proceeding to eat. He once instructed his descendants, saying:

"If the wealth and grain of our household are sufficient, you should consider yourselves fortunate; do not be arrogant or indulge in excessive luxury and self-indulgence. This further reveals the character of this man.
At the beginning of the first year of the Yuanyou era, he suddenly felt moved within himself, saying: "It is time for me to depart," and thereupon ceased consuming meat and blood.
The Master continued his recitation until the third month, yet his countenance remained undisturbed; he joined his fingers in a mudrā and passed away suddenly at the age of ninety-three.

The following year, on an auspicious day in the second month, he was buried in the southwestern corner of the district. Having once visited this district, I was informed of these events by his orphans, who wailed and prostrated themselves, requesting me to compose an inscription for his tomb. The inscription reads: The Buddha’s teaching reached him for three months, yet his spirit remained unconfused. Joining his fingers in a seal, he suddenly departed from the world. He attained the age of ninety-three. In the following year, on an auspicious day in the second month, he was interred in the southwestern corner of the district.
I once passed through this district when the orphans described his deeds to me; they wailed and bowed their heads, entreating me to write this epitaph. The epitaph says:
Alas, that noble gentleman, Renowned throughout his village and district, Was born through uprightness And died with a full span of life.
Having a beginning and an end, Perfect in every way and beautiful, He bequeathed his plans to his descendants; Truly, his legacy shall never cease.
This concludes the extensive presentation of the *Lijing* records of the Ma family.
The laywoman Ma, a faithful follower of the Dharma, was a native of Guanchen Town in Haiyan County, Xiuzhou. Her father’s name was Xisheng; she was naturally gentle and compliant from birth.

Having married Chen Shihua, a man of the town, she personally attended to her domestic duties with diligence and brought harmony to her kin. Through the roots of merit she had planted in former lives, she devoted herself earnestly to the Buddhist faith.
She delighted in goodness and took pity on all things, being frugal in her own use while generous in her giving. Whenever monks or Daoists passed by her door, even those who were solitary...

Whenever those seeking an audience came during the cold season, he was always able to set aside his own needs to provide for whatever others desired. When he reached the age of thirty, he suddenly attained a realization;
he then lamented that the retribution of women is extremely base and turbid, and he grew deeply weary of this toilsome life, finding nothing in it worth enjoying. He said:

"The light of years passes away easily, yet a meager fate is difficult to preserve. If one merely indulges in worldly pleasures and does not exert oneself in cultivation, then one day one will go forever."
On this journey, what can he rely on for his preservation? Though jade is precious, it cannot prolong one's life; how could even the closest kin replace him?
For this reason, he cast aside worldly affairs and swept his chamber clean, vowing to take the recitation of Buddhist scriptures as his daily practice.

With incense and lamps burning day after day, he applied himself with tireless diligence until the onset of old age, serving with ever-increasing devotion. Regarding whatever sutras or liturgical services he encountered, he made no distinction between their scale or grandeur.

He practiced approximately one prostration for each character, so that over the years the count grew until it filled volumes; when comparing the number of characters to the prostrations, they were truly beyond counting.
Furthermore, he regularly observed the six fasts (*ṣaḍ-vrata*) throughout his life without fail, and having repeatedly received the five and eight precepts, he maintained them with great rigor.
In the middle of the summer during the fifth year of the Yuanfeng era, while suffering from a slight illness that did not abate, he suddenly saw a śramaṇa approach with palms joined in reverence.
In an instant he vanished. At noon the following day, looking back at his attendants, he asked, "Is it now midday?
Then, seeing a śramaṇa approaching and beckoning him forward, he adjusted his appearance, sat in the full lotus posture, and forming mudrās with his fingers, passed away in a flash.
This was the seventeenth day of that month; he had reached the age of sixty-six and fathered three sons: the eldest was named Weizhao, the second Weigong, and the youngest... [died young].

The deceased’s younger sister, named Zheng, followed; all three daughters had already been married off. On the twenty-first day of the first month of the following year, she was buried in Huatong Township of her native district.
Her sons wailed and lamented, saying, "Our compassionate mother accumulated many virtuous deeds worthy of being heard, yet we have been unable to give them due praise;
this is not the way of filial piety. They therefore recorded the facts of her life and requested a preface from me.
Shi-zhi said to me: "The teaching of our Buddha is vast and far-reaching, benefiting all without exception.

There are none among it—whether man or woman, noble or lowly, old or young, wise or foolish—who do not reach it. Indeed, there are those who possess profound faith and those who practice it with their own bodies;
thus, within the state of non-attainment, there is nothing that is not attained. From its origins, such instances have certainly not been few."

As for the case of Lady Ma, although her practice of Buddhism is not fully known in its details or profundity, considering that she was virtuous throughout her life and met a peaceful end, one may say she attained something of value.
Confucians claim that women and "small people" (servants) are difficult to sustain; however, I believe one cannot judge a person by their class, for it lies solely in their will.
Furthermore, there are those who are immature and untamable, yet even they—though [otherwise] incapable—[may achieve this].
If one can be taught yet cannot maintain self-restraint, they will be unable to fully provide for their parents, nor will they be able to fully demonstrate loyalty to their ruler.
Greedy with wealth, debauched by beauty, intoxicated by wine, and addicted to music, they remain muddled and empty all day long until the end of their lives.
Though such a person may be a man, he is no true man; though she may be a woman, she is no true woman. Even those of later generations who examine this would find it unacceptable.
How I sigh in admiration! The Buddhist Records of the Sun Family of Siming:
The laywoman of the Sun family from Qingxin, Siming, Cixi, having become a widow in middle age, grew weary of worldly habits and discarded her feminine ornaments.
He was solely devoted to the Buddha-dharma for over thirty years, maintaining a vegetarian diet, observing the precepts, and engaging in recitation and liturgy without ceasing until old age.
He constantly fashioned robes, shrouds, socks, and shoes with his own hands to bestow upon the Sangha, the total number of which remained unknown.

Whenever there were offerings or assemblies, he would personally attend to the duties to manifest his utmost reverence. He sent his son to follow the teachings of Śākyamuni, saying: "Let Ru Bian reside at Mount Zhi in meditative concentration."
Huìlán happened to be building a meditation hut at his original residence, which was located in a noisy and bustling area;
he therefore went to reside where Huàn was staying for nearly half a year. Regarding all monastic requisites, including even tea and water, Huìlán never once consumed them.

At that time, Huàn was planning a three-year long repentance ceremony to fulfill a vow, and he personally supervised Huìlán’s conduct, not tolerating any negligence or laxity. Huàn was somewhat intimidated by him; suddenly, he frequently dreamed of the Buddha.
The monk applied himself with even greater diligence. One day, while slightly ill, he saw a strange person standing before his bed who addressed him, saying:
"You should recite the scriptures with constant devotion; you must not be negligent. Subsequently, he dreamed that eight monks were circumambulating his repentance chamber;

he saw himself wearing a *kaṣāya* robe and following the monks as they performed their devotions. After a short while, he again saw a wooden shrine in the center, its lacquer finish bright and lustrous.
Upon awakening, he realized that the signs of his impending departure had appeared; he then instructed the monks to perform repentance and recitation, saying, "I shall return to the Pure Land.
He dismissed his relatives, commanding them not to disturb him, and sought fragrant water for a bath.

Having donned clean robes, he sat cross-legged before the assembly, bound his hands in mudrā, and took up his prayer beads and banners. He recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* until reaching the words, "single-mindedly without distraction."
Fen said, "Help me recite this; my breath is nearly spent. Having finished speaking, he passed away suddenly. A wondrous fragrance and celestial music were heard by those both near and far.
His body remained for seven days, after which his fellow villagers gathered fragrant wood to cremate him. His remains were interred at a certain mountain.

At the age of seventy-eight, during his daily life, he had recorded the number of times he performed prostrations, recited scriptures, and worshipped the Buddha. This is now carved upon stone and preserved here.
In future generations, may those who behold this know that the Buddha-dharma cannot but be believed; once believed, it cannot but be practiced;

and once practiced, virtuous signs will surely follow. Thus they shall know that the retribution of cause and effect regarding fortune and misfortune is like a shadow following a form or a seal matching its imprint, without the slightest discrepancy. How can those who hear or see this fail to exert themselves?

On the [blank] day of the [blank] month, I, the monk Yuanzhao, having reverently purified myself through incense and washing, respectfully compose this letter to be presented to Your Honor, the Commissioner of the Regional Administration.
Since my childhood, I have left the household life; upon reaching the age of capping, I sat for the examinations and attained success. Furthermore...
Having shaved my head and received the precepts, I have devoted myself to the Buddha-vehicle for sixteen years.

Although I am of mediocre and dull capacity, I have diligently applied myself to the scrolls and volumes; though I cannot yet penetrate the profound depths of the Sage’s treasury, I have roughly grasped one or two parts in ten thousand.
Now, despite the risk of appearing frivolous and unrefined, I venture to speak thus to you: as for the Buddha’s teaching, it generally points toward...
The myriad transformations return to the one mind; by means of the one mind, one perceives one's own nature. Furthermore, as for the substance of this nature:
it is profoundly still, vast and empty, luminously penetrating and unimpeded. Its height cannot be surpassed, and its breadth has no limit.

Within it, there are neither Buddhas nor sentient beings, neither the primary body nor the attendant manifestations, neither birth nor death, neither coming nor going, neither folly nor wisdom, and neither things nor self.

Equal, of one mark, and that one mark being markless—this is called the Dharma-realm, the eternally abiding, True Suchness, the Real Mark, the Tathāgatagarbha, Śūraṅgama, Prajñā, and Nirvāṇa; these various different names are in fact one.
The Sage awakens to it and calls it Bodhi; sentient beings are deluded by it and call it affliction.

The Sage, by means of that which he has awakened to, awakens those who are still in darkness; thus, though formless, he manifests a hundred billion countenances and demeanors, and though unspeakable, he proclaims the sutras of the great trichiliocosm.
As capacities differ among various classes of beings, the teachings follow diverse paths;
yet, when one examines where they all converge, they do not exceed the Three Piṭakas—namely, the Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma—which demonstrate what is to be cultivated.
Thus, there are the three trainings, namely: precepts (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). Precepts serve to regulate the body and speech;
concentration and wisdom serve to refine and transform one's nature and temperament.

Yet, those who ascend the distant heights do not begin anywhere other than from the near, and those who enter the inner chamber do not do so without passing through the door. Therefore, among the Three Pitakas and the Three Trainings, one must prioritize the precepts.
The Vinaya is the foremost; in the past, Master Nanshan took this study as his own responsibility, wielding the brush to compose works and vigorously propagate its essentials.
His collected writings comprise more than three hundred fascicles.

Although I am not gifted, I have formerly devoted myself to this school and thus know that the precepts are the ship and oar for crossing the sea of suffering and the source from which all myriad virtues arise.
This is the beginning of the path revered by the sages and worthies of the Three Vehicles and transmitted through the ancestral masters of successive generations.
However, because those who receive it vary in the clarity of their minds and the refinement of their studies, they cannot all be judged by a single standard;

thus, there are those who receive it for the first time and those who increase their practice further. Therefore, the Vinaya clarifies that the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) consists of three grades: the first is that which aspires solely to liberation.
First, to single-mindedly seek one's own benefit is called the inferior grade; this is the mind of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).

Second, to resolve the doubts of others for the sake of benefiting both self and others is called the middling grade; this is the mind of a minor bodhisattva. Third, to forget oneself to benefit living beings, to practice merit and wisdom in tandem, to realize the fundamental nature, and to seek the Buddha’s enlightenment is called the superior grade; this is the mind of a great bodhisattva.

The mind clearly knows that what was initially received was only of the middle or lower grade; the Buddha opened the way for it to be further increased and transformed into the superior grade—this is what is called "increasing the precepts" (*vṛddha-śīla*).

According to the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Liang Dynasty*, in the eleventh year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, a foreign monk named Saṃghavarman, while crossing the banks of the Cai River by boat, [encountered] Huìyì and about fifty others at Qihuan Temple.

Regarding the re-initiation of the precepts within the river: furthermore, according to the *Jietan tu jing* (Diagram of the Precept Platform), in the second year of the Qianfeng era of the Tang dynasty, the Vinaya Master of Nanshan performed the rite of receiving the precepts again during both the spring and summer seasons for śramaṇas from various mountains and rivers.

Thus, the *Sifen lü* (Four-Part Vinaya), the *Chengshi lun* (Tattvasiddhi Śāstra), and the various records of the lineage of masters and disciples all clarify the method of re-initiation; this is indeed the true Buddhist tradition.
This is merely the constant ritual and the fundamental practice of the monastic community;

yet, there is indeed a reason why those masters, unaware of its true significance, incite one another with delusions, engage in strife, and create such turmoil. During the Xining era, I returned from my travels through Wenzhou and Taizhou to my home monastery.
My quarters were located in the southeastern corner of Xiangfu Temple, where I shut my door to devote myself exclusively to my studies, declining all visitors.
While attending to human affairs, I took advantage of moments of leisure to wield the fly-whisk and extol the precepts and regulations;
before long, my reputation spread, and friends from distant regions began arriving daily with their satchels to study under me.

I have long been concerned that the True Dharma is in decline, that human sentiments have grown base and shallow, and that the monastic leadership has been frayed for no small number of days. Thus, disregarding my own limitations, I have harbored the intention to provide support and restoration. Therefore—
Now, those who come must broaden their minds through dhyāna and wisdom and constrain themselves with the laws and precepts.

Carrying alms bowls to beg for food to satisfy their stomachs, and sewing coarse cloth into garments to cover their bodies, they increase their hardships day by day and intensify their efforts night after night.

Whether in seclusion or in society, whether speaking or remaining silent, they follow the Buddha’s regulations in all matters. For several years in this manner, they have not dared to be negligent; yet, as they were about to—

When one follows the ancient path, it inevitably runs counter to common sentiments; often, one's peers regard this as affectation and eccentricity, and there are even those who watch for such conduct to look for faults and shortcomings.
I offer this private explanation: Confucius said, "If one serves his ruler with the utmost ritual propriety, others will consider him sycophantic.
Now, I serve the Buddha with the utmost sincerity, yet people consider me deceitful—is this not only to be expected? Furthermore, Confucius was a sage.
It is said that although he had no verbal transgressions and his conduct was free from resentment or malice, he could not yet avoid the hatred and jealousy of the secular world;
thus, he was suspected by Huan Tai, disgraced by Yang Hu, threatened by the people of Kuang, and distressed between Chen and Cai.

How much less, then, can an ordinary monk at the very bottom of the ranks—who studies antiquity while turning his back on the secular world—hope to avoid being hated by others? This is why [it has come to this].
Those followers, due to differences in their conduct and affairs, harbored resentment from long ago;
they then took advantage of the momentum of this increase in precepts to instigate strife and litigation. Their intention was nothing other than to cast innocent people into fetters.
Reflecting on this, I consider myself out of step with the times, entirely lacking in influential support, and unable to overcome the multitude by my own strength alone.

I respectfully consider that you, the Honorable Administrator and Commissioner, possess the talents of Yi Yin and Zhou Gong to assist a sovereign like Yao or Shun;

your literary reputation and administrative skill stand preeminent among the multitude of elites, and your benevolent governance and virtuous influence descend upon all things. I pray that you will deign to...

That which is shown by the Buddhas of Dhyāna consists of these three; all emerge from the Buddha, who spoke of the Three Studies and the Six Perfections.

Therefore, one who acts as a Buddha must not be obstructed by a single aspect. Proper deportment, ritual measures, prohibitions and transgressions, and permissions and restrictions are all seen in the Vinaya;

without study, there is no means to clarify them for oneself. Expedient and ultimate, partial and complete, contemplative practices, and cause and effect are all seen in the Śāstras; without study, [one cannot understand them].

Without study, one cannot awaken for oneself. As the Sūtra says: "The source to which one returns is non-dual, yet the skillful means have many gates.

Thus, Vinaya, Teaching, and Chan emerge from the same origin but bear different names; they follow divergent paths yet share a single thread. What is meant by "emerging from the same origin" is that they all arise from the One Mind.

That which is "all-pervasive" (yìguàn) is the convergence in the single nature, which is the mind-nature. This mind-nature is the essence of awakening and cognition present before all sentient beings.
Its measure is empty and still; its function is vast and pervasive. It lies latent within the boundaries of the myriad transformations and is manifest within the midst of active functioning.
Though the four marks flow on, it does not shift; though the three delusions cover it, it constantly shines. Alas, how can bubbles arise?
The ocean of awakening is like a vast expanse of clouds; when a single speck lands on the shore of Great Purity, the boat shifts with it.

Flowers bloom because of optical illusions, and intense deluded movement arises from dense ignorance and obstruction, scattering in confusion for neither one morning nor one evening. Our Buddha took pity on them, intending to cause them to return to their original nature.
Thus, he regulated their deluded movements—hence the term *vinaya* (precepts)—and opened up their dense obstructions—hence the term *dharma* (teachings).

Because it gathers together that which is wandering and scattered, it is called *dhyāna* (meditation). Viewed from this perspective, the precepts (*vinaya*) are also the mind; the teachings (*śāsana*) are also the mind; and meditation is also the mind.
Since all three are my own mind, how could there be room for judgments of right and wrong, or self and other, within them?
Otherwise, if there were dharmas existing outside the mind, one would not have realized the intent of the Supreme Vehicle of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Therefore, since antiquity...
In their knowledge and conduct, they have never failed to be grounded in the Vinaya; in their extensive study of the sutras and śāstras, they have never failed to understand the teachings;
and in their pursuit of the profound and subtle, their serenity, they have never failed to penetrate Zen.

Surveying the Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Three Dynasties, one finds those who ate only wood and wore only grass, whose solitary integrity and asceticism stood out so prominently that the wind and frost could not alter their character, and whose resolute resolve remained unshaken by sorrow.
Because Xī had not yet fully realized his mind’s intent, he was able to establish a pure reputation in his time and leave a lasting model for the historical records.

mistaking license for universal liberation and deriding steadfast observance as attachment to forms; thus destroying the true teaching and clouding the eyes of future generations—the Tripiṭaka Master felt profound compassion.
It is for this reason that this collection of writings was composed; it is truly intended to remedy the errors and defects of the time and to protect the fundamental principles of the Buddha-dharma.

Moreover, whether refuting one position to establish another, or tempering excess by elevating what is deficient, is the universal rule for composition within the Śākya school and the constant practice of scholarly inquiry into doctrine.

Thus, the various treatises of the Western Heaven (India) attack one another, whether they belong to the Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna, or whether they contend over emptiness (*śūnyatā*) or existence (*astitva*).

The various schools—such as the two divisions, five divisions, eighteen schools, and five hundred divergent sects—have been locked in fierce opposition regarding their fundamental nature and characteristics;

these fragmented and divergent tenets persist to this day without end. In this land of China, the transmission of the teachings has seen the *Avataṃsaka*, Xianshou, Tiantai, and Cien schools mutually contesting one another, with their commentaries and treatises vying for preeminence.

This is much like the Confucian tradition, where the *Spring and Autumn Annals* of the Lu state opened up into five successive transmissions, and the *Gao*, *Feng*, *Ya*, and *Song* sections were divided into distinct lineages.
Regarding the four schools of poetry, Mencius’s words were set apart from those of Yang Zhu and Mo Di; Master Yun took nothing from Laozi and Zhuangzi.

Zheng Xuan and Wang Su engaged in discourse as teacher and disciple that was as contradictory as a physical paradox, while Liu Xiang and Liu Xin, father and son, held differing opinions on the same matters.
As for our own school, since the arrival of Bodhidharma from the West and the transmission of the robe and bowl down to the Fifth Patriarch, there arose the divisions of North and South.
Subsequently, they divided into schools, each establishing its own tradition; thus, the five houses branched out, with Yunmen and Linji flourishing in their time.

Yet, each adhered strictly to its own lineage while mutually deriding the others. They disparaged listening and learning as...

This is surely because they do not understand that the ancient sages, out of deep compassion for all beings, employed skillful means and bitter words to lead seekers toward the fish by means of the moon, so that they would not remain stuck to the trap or the finger.
As for me, the poor monk, I left my kin in my youth and attained the age of capping.
Since I first sought out my teacher to pursue my studies, carrying my books on a staff and holding the scriptures across my chest, thirty-one years have passed.
Unexpectedly, being of meager virtue, I was mistakenly appointed as a head teacher. In every place I have nurtured disciples, instructing them morning and night;

above, I seek to repay the grace of the Buddhas and Patriarchs who brought me enlightenment, and below, I seek to requite the merit of the kings and ministers who have protected and sustained the Dharma. Recently, the former Governor, Lord Wang Xiuzhen, held [the precepts]...

The ancient texts were compiled in old records, yet I, of meager learning, failed to recognize this and instead harbored private resentment, even going so far as to lodge a lawsuit with the government offices and confront the high officials, desiring to cast him into a deep pit and weigh him down with great stones. Through such intimidation and coercion, he nearly could not escape.
I reflect privately that there is an ancient saying: "What comes forth from you will return to you. Since I have already been without intent toward him...
How could external things possibly add anything to me? Therefore, I have remained silent and sat watching, never once uttering a word to defend myself.

Yet, fearing that the official authorities may not yet fully comprehend the true circumstances, I have respectfully brought the original ancient manuscript of my collected works along with its preface detailing the beginning and end of the matter to your presence.
Whether it be right or wrong, whether it be just or unjust, I leave it solely to your honorable judgment, sir. Yours sincerely.
Letter Accompanying the Robe and Alms Bowl.
On the [day] of the [month], the Bhikṣu Yuánzhào respectfully composes this letter to present to the Chan Master Yuánzhào of Jìngcí.
Early in my life, I studied the Vinaya and learned that the Buddha’s regulations require a bhikṣu to be fully provided with the three [robes].

The robes, the alms bowl, the sitting mat, and the water filter constitute the six articles; these were established for those of superior, middling, and inferior faculties to ensure they are observed and honored.
One who follows this path must not willfully transgress them; to do so would be to oppose the supreme instruction and is contrary to what is called the way of teacher and disciple.
What are the three robes? The first is the *saṃghāṭī*, also called the great robe, which one should wear when entering a village to receive offerings.

The second is the *uttarāsaṅga*, called the "upper robe," which is worn when ascending the seat to preach the Dharma, during communal liturgical recitations, or when entering the hall to receive food.
The third is the *antarvāsaka*, called the "lower robe," which is worn when traveling on roads or performing tasks within the monastery.
These three types of robes must necessarily be made of coarse materials such as hemp or ramie.
Its substance is dark blue-black, dyed with mūlāñjana; it measures three or five cubits in length. It is torn apart and then sewn back together to quell greedy desires;
its branches and leaves are clearly distinct to demonstrate the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). Regarding its appearance, it is modeled after the sages of the Three Vehicles;
regarding its name, it is something unheard of among the ninety-six heterodox paths; and regarding its efficacy, [it is beyond compare].

Thus, people may escape the anxiety of misfortune and peril, and dragons may avoid the calamity of being carried off by the *garuḍa*. These matters are fully preserved in the various great treasuries of scripture and cannot be cited here exhaustively.
Regarding the single bowl: its full name is *pātra*, which is translated as "proper vessel. It may be made of either iron or earthenware; the substance must conform to the Dharma.
It should be smoke-stained and possess a deep green hue; this color must conform to the Dharma. Its capacity should be three *dōng* or two and a half *dōng*.
The Dharma is indeed the insignia of all Buddhas, rather than a mere utensil for the halls of state.
Formerly, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa bestowed upon me, the original teacher Śākyamuni, the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, which refers to this thirteen-piece coarse cloth *saṃghāṭī*.
Upon approaching his parinirvāṇa, he dispatched the Venerable Kāśyapa to hold it at Mount Kukkuṭapāda to await [my arrival].

Maitreya has a reason for regarding the Buddha as the one most worthy of veneration; that the Patriarchs traveled westward and transmitted the Dharma through six generations serves as a testament to the succession of the Dharma, which has been the highest priority for each successive patriarch.
Now, there is a monk who was among the disciples at the lecture hall, who for many years has faithfully maintained his monastic requisites.
Recently, having fallen ill, he passed away; as he was about to open his hands and feet [in death], he entrusted me with his robes.
I respectfully offer this alms bowl and sitting mat to the Chan Master, truly relying upon his compassionate protection to aid me on my path beyond the grave.

I humbly reflect that the Master’s realization of the Way surpasses those who came before, and his virtue encompasses all things. Monks and laypeople alike flock to him like swarms of ants, and followers from near and far converge like clouds.

Among the monasteries throughout the land, none can rival such prosperity. I venture to say that affairs are undertaken according to the times, and the Way is propagated through individuals; may you indeed grant us a brief respite.
I humbly entreat Your Eminence to condescend to my lowly intent and grant me your acceptance; I shall specially uphold it as such.

In this way, the solemn regulations of the Great Sage may be put into practice, and the bequeathed tradition of the Patriarchs shall not fall into ruin. I have respectfully dispatched a monk carrying robes and bowl—the five requisites—to deliver this letter and convey my purpose.
Whether you grant or decline this request, I leave it entirely to the Chan Master’s discretion. I do not further elaborate. Sincerely yours, [Name].
Question: Are calumny (*chán*) and slander (*bàng*) the same or different? Answer: Calumny necessarily relies upon slander to be accomplished.
There may be slander that does not constitute calumny, but one has never seen calumny that does not involve slander. As for the arising of calumny, its origin begins with hatred.
To harbor jealousy yet ultimately act upon it out of misplaced trust is the way of the sycophantic and petty man.
Among the ancients, there were those who offered loyalty to assist their sovereigns, practiced filial piety to serve their parents, and embraced righteousness to bond with friends;
yet, though they enjoyed the harmony of ruler and subject, the affection of father and son, or the intimacy of friends, if on a single day they were slandered by someone—

When eyes turn against one another and arms are rolled up in defiance, leading to expulsion, alienation, and estrangement until they regard each other as enemies, even the ancient sages and worthies could not avoid such a fate.
Among these, there are cases where the truth cannot be discerned at first but becomes clear only after a long time;
those where it cannot be discerned while alive but becomes clear after death; and those where it cannot be discerned until death and remains unclarified for all eternity—this is unavoidable.
"Excessive frequency is worse than nothing," said Ziyou. "To be too frequent in serving one's ruler brings disgrace; to be too frequent with friends leads to estrangement.

This was intended as a warning for people to distance themselves from slander. Alas! Slander and defamation must be scrutinized. Moreover, they are recorded in the Classics and Histories so that they are not obscure;
yet when scholars read them, there are none who do not know their wrongfulness, yet they often personally fall into them nonetheless.
Those whose slanderous mouths choke them until death, unable to clear their own names, do so because the one who receives the slander fails to perceive the flattery and insincerity of the slanderer.
When a group of petty people come before him and further slander others, he listens again and takes it to be true;
can this be called being wise? Indeed, those skilled at slandering are clever and artful at inciting strife and creating discord.

To flatter and deceive someone until they become so bewildered that they appear as if possessed by a demon—such that there are those who cannot perceive the truth for the rest of their lives—Confucius said:
"The slander of gradual seepage and the accusations of immediate sensory provocation. As for the coming of this gradual seepage, it does not allow people to anticipate it;
even though Zeng Shen was of supreme filial piety, his mother would still have suspected him of murder. In a marketplace that is not a secluded forest, anyone will surely [be suspected].
Suspecting that there might be tigers [in the path], some occasionally do not proceed; such individuals may be called enlightened and far-sighted gentlemen.

As for me, being foolish, clumsy, and indolent, I have no fondness for flattery or fawning upon others, nor do I seek to please them falsely; consequently, I have frequently been the subject of slander and calumny by others.
Upon hearing this, I reflect in private, saying: "If what they say is indeed true, I ought to reform my faults; then they are my teachers."
He says, "Is this not the fruit? But his words are merely empty; how could they defile me? Thus, though my ears hear him, my mouth has never debated with him.
Whether a scholar or gentleman perceives or does not perceive depends on whether their talent and insight are clear or obscure.
How could I go about asserting what is wrong or right by seeking approval from others? Yet, even if one does not know at first, after a long time it will become clear.
"Will it become clear in a future age, or will it remain obscure forever? Wen Zhongzi said, "How does one stop slander?
By not defending oneself. I have often acted upon these words."
Regarding the "Discourse on Board Games" (*Bóyì jiè*): The *Analects* states, "To eat one's fill all day long without applying one's mind—how difficult this is! Is there not board games?
To engage in them is still better than doing nothing at all. The commentary says: This was Confucius encouraging people to pursue learning; it was not intended to...
Regarding people playing games: what distinguishes ordinary humans from grasses, trees, stones, and soil is that they possess consciousness;
what distinguishes them from birds and beasts is that they are the most spiritually endowed;
what distinguishes them from the common crowd is that they engage in learning; and what distinguishes them from their peers is that they exert themselves with ceaseless vigor.
Therefore, as a person, one cannot fail to engage in learning; and in engaging in learning, one cannot fail to exert oneself.
How could it be appropriate to eat one’s fill and wander about in idle play, remaining ignorant of learning and becoming indistinguishable from the common crowd?

Even if one does study, if there is no accomplishment, will one’s achievements not remain no different from those of one's peers? Since antiquity, the sages and worthies have been urgent in their pursuit of learning, striving with tireless diligence.
When there is leisure for other matters, one still fears wasting time; yet even in the shadows of such haste, there are things one fails to reach.

How much more so for those who are utterly oblivious and lack any application of mind, drifting aimlessly until they grow old—how do they know how to compose themselves, or how to pass their long days?
This is why the Sage sighed in lamentation, saying: "How difficult it is! Were it not for those who engage in board games..."
"To do this is still better than doing nothing"— this comparison uses the lowly affairs of the marketplace to contrast them with one another,
intending to cause people to feel shame and think of pursuing learning. Furthermore, while gathering in groups to gamble and compete for victory is hardly something a worthy person should do,
if one applies their mind to it, even an unworthy person can be considered worthy by virtue of seeing it through to completion.
Those who consume their lives in vain without applying themselves to learning do not even equal the petty men of gambling; how much less could they be considered gentlemen?
This was intended as a profound exhortation, not as a praise of games of chance meant to encourage people to engage in them.
How could the teaching of a Sage ever lead people toward unrighteousness? The Confucian commentators say: "It is because [the game] has no basis and offers no pleasure."
"Because they give rise to lustful desires, I merely have them engage in gambling.
This not only destroys the intent of the sages' teachings and casts people into unrighteousness, but how vulgar and base his words are!
Every time I read this, I cannot help but sigh in lamentation. Even He Pingshu still considers [the views of] various schools...

Even those among the virtuous, such as Huang Kan and Xing Bǐng, were unable to examine whether these works were sound or not; they merely followed established tradition without offering correction or rectification.
Consequently, scholars from ancient times to the present—wearing the scholar’s cap or the monastic robe—vied with one another to practice *bóyì* (games of chance) as a personal skill.
They often abandoned their studies and neglected worldly affairs, losing themselves day and night, forgetting to eat and sleep, until their spirits were utterly exhausted.
His eyesight and physical strength grew weary and exhausted until he fell ill; yet, still not knowing when to stop, he ultimately achieved nothing beneficial.
Furthermore, when benevolent men and gentlemen act or speak, they must first examine whether it will cause harm or benefit before proceeding.
Why then do you allow yourself to be driven by worldly arts without considering this? I have once spoken to him at length to urge him [to change], but he rejected me, saying:
Confucius was still praised as a worthy son; why then have you, in your ignorance, incurred this reproach?

I have therefore retired to reflect that the errors of former scholars have misled those who followed them, which is not a small matter. Thus, I have specially provided this alternative interpretation, hoping that gentlemen of discernment may perhaps find it useful.
Preface to the Essential Words of the Four Sons on the Way of Heaven:
The essence of the Way of Heaven is firmness while its function is flexibility; the essence of the Way of Earth is flexibility while its function is firmness.

Humans, born between heaven and earth, receive the two qi of heaven and earth to form their substance; they ought, therefore, to model their conduct upon heaven and earth. The sage-kings of antiquity were able to...

Exhausting the principles of Heaven and Earth, one models oneself on the flexibility of Heaven to teach people how to practice benevolence (*ren*), and models oneself on the firmness of Earth to teach people how to act with righteousness (*yi*).
Therefore, benevolence centers on compassionate love, while righteousness centers on resolute decisiveness;
these are the great foundation of human relations and the ultimate pinnacle of Confucian teaching. Confucius followed the legacy of Yao and Shun and established the statutes of Wen and Wu.
What else could Master Wu have meant? Thus it is said: "My Way is unified by a single thread; it is simply loyalty and reciprocity. Is loyalty not righteousness (*yi*)?

Is reciprocity not benevolence (*ren*)? From this we know that although Confucius’s speech and action, movement and stillness, and his various applications may differ in myriad ways, they never depart from benevolence and righteousness.
I have perused the writings of the various masters, and among them, I alone cherish those of Xunzi, Mencius, Yangzi, and Wangzi.
Being able to take the Way of Confucius as his primary tenet and understand the foundation of the Ruist teaching, Mencius said to King Hui of Liang:
"Why must you speak only of profit? There need only be benevolence and righteousness. Wenzhongzi said: "Benevolence and righteousness are the foundation of instruction. Xunzi said:
"One must only maintain benevolence and only practice righteousness. Yangzi said: "The *Taixuan* is benevolence."
It is precisely because they were composed with such righteousness that the *Four Books* of the Master are not confused with heterodox teachings.
While the *Mencius* and the *Analects* were recorded by the Master’s disciples, the *Xunzi* and the *Yangzi* were compiled by the authors themselves;

their prose is rich and their subject matter extensive, such that they cannot be fully surveyed without one who has extensively mastered the Confucian tradition. Therefore, from among them, I have selected what is concise and appropriate.
These essential words, sufficient for instructing the world, have been compiled into a single collection titled *The Essential Words of the Four Sons*.

Although these words are concise, they fully encompass the principles of learning, the Way, human conduct, and governance, as well as the duties between ruler and subject and father and son, and the ten thousand practices and five constant virtues.
If one studies them and reflects upon them, will they not surely benefit one’s mind and character?
Preface to the *Lèdào jí* of Minister of State Yi of Goryeo:
In the past, when I encountered envoys from海东 (Haidong) passing through my native region, I observed that they frequently composed verses on the famous mountains and scenic landmarks there;
judging by their style and refinement, these were largely consistent with the literary traditions of the Great Country. Later, I encountered the writings left behind by the Chief Monk (Sengtǒng).
The phrasing was plain yet the underlying meaning was profound; furthermore, he realized that the Master-General of the Sangha was also a deep connoisseur of poetry.
Later, while returning from the court to Hangzhou and mooring his boat at Fuheng, he suddenly encountered the collected poems of Prime Minister Li, which were presented to him.

Upon opening the volume and reading it through, he admired how the author’s learning was vast and his insight far-reaching, and how the diction was direct yet the principles reached their ultimate refinement. For the most part, they were modeled upon the Buddhist scriptures and followed their essential tenets.
His discourse on the principle of nature transcends all mundane affairs; it is not what is called secular literary composition.
Because he aspired to true stillness while dwelling in wealth and honor, he titled his work "Delighting in the Way" (Lèdào).

Because he maintained pure integrity while living amidst worldly defilement, he designated himself by the title "Upāsaka. Since the Way is omnipresent, his words were inspired by whatever circumstance he encountered.

As for the nature of things, they should be preserved in their general outlines; recording even a hundred pieces is sufficient to propagate and praise the Buddha-vehicle and to enlighten future generations.
How could this be compared to those who engage in the trivial art of calligraphy or the mere chanting of wind and moon?

Nevertheless, although there are many scholars in that country capable of composing poetry, the Head Monk alone has cherished this collection and intends to have it carved onto printing blocks for circulation.
This is universally recognized; what was previously called the "Monastic Head" (Sengtong) being profoundly knowledgeable of poetry is indeed not false.
Those who contemplate this poem should embody this meaning.
Preface to the Farewell of Wen Bolong upon His Return to the Imperial Academy.

Beyond my study of Buddhism, I have often perused the works of the former Confucian scholars. Observing how the ancient sages established their words and transmitted their laws, it appears they primarily intended for people to cultivate themselves, rectify their natures, establish their persons, and practice the Way, thereby distinguishing themselves from the common masses.

Yet, alas, the scholars of later generations differ in the purity or shallowness of their innate dispositions and the level of their training; though all read the books and call themselves Confucians, there remains a divergence.
Among those who practice it, there are those who truly cultivate it and those who do not; thus, the gentleman and the petty man are distinguished.
Confucius said to Zi Xia, "Be a gentleman scholar; do not be a petty scholar. Those who study the Ru classics today recite their texts in no small measure.
When they engage in debate, their discourse is clear and worthy of being heard; when they produce writings, they are rich and elegant to behold. However—
Proud of his own talent and refinement, he was frivolous, arrogant, and dissolute; there was no excess to which he would not resort.

Consequently, those who sought him as a gentleman-scholar were few indeed. I had never previously known him, yet I had heard from elders that his character and conduct were praiseworthy and that his contemporaries admired his literary achievements. When I finally met him, I listened to his words and observed his actions.
It is exactly as I have heard; whenever I spoke with others, I would say that this is what is called a "gentleman-scholar" (junzi ru), and it is only fitting that such a person should be esteemed.
Having recently heard that he is preparing his luggage to return to the National University, I have recorded these words directly to encourage him, hoping they may serve as some small benefit.
Preface to the Collected Works of Chan Master Changlu Ze:

That which the Buddhist teachings call a Mahāyāna master refers to a man of superior faculties, keen intelligence, and courageous resolve who, through sudden realization, understands his own mind and comprehensively penetrates all phenomena.
He realizes that all things arise through conditions and lack inherent nature, that everything is thusness, and that this conditionality and lack of inherent nature constitute a vast expanse.
